claim: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight in both male and female mice.
source: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight (A), fat mass (B), lean mass (C), and tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach (D) in both males and female mice, and was further accentuated following 48 hr restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: 18 hr food restriction reduced fat mass in both male and female mice.
source: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight (A), fat mass (B), lean mass (C), and tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach (D) in both males and female mice, and was further accentuated following 48 hr restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: 18 hr food restriction reduced lean mass in both male and female mice.
source: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight (A), fat mass (B), lean mass (C), and tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach (D) in both males and female mice, and was further accentuated following 48 hr restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: 18 hr food restriction reduced tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach in both male and female mice.
source: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight (A), fat mass (B), lean mass (C), and tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach (D) in both males and female mice, and was further accentuated following 48 hr restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D and described in the text.

claim: 48 hr food restriction further accentuated the reduction in body weight, fat mass, lean mass, and tissue weights compared to 18 hr restriction.
source: 18 hr food restriction reduced body weight (A), fat mass (B), lean mass (C), and tissue weights of inguinal WAT, epididymal WAT, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach (D) in both males and female mice, and was further accentuated following 48 hr restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing 18 hr and 48 hr fasting conditions shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: Withholding food access overnight robustly decreased body weight, fat mass and lean mass in every mouse, independent of sex.
source: Withholding food access overnight robustly decreased body weight, fat mass and lean mass in every mouse, independent of sex; these effects were exacerbated in the 48 hr food-deprived condition (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The effects of food deprivation on body weight, fat mass and lean mass were exacerbated in the 48 hr food-deprived condition.
source: Withholding food access overnight robustly decreased body weight, fat mass and lean mass in every mouse, independent of sex; these effects were exacerbated in the 48 hr food-deprived condition (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Increasing levels of food-deprivation reliably reduced weights of both inguinal and epididymal white adipose tissue, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach tissue.
source: We also found that increasing levels of food-deprivation reliably reduced weights of both inguinal and epididymal white adipose tissue, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, liver and stomach tissue (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Fasting appreciably lowered concentrations of glucose, triacylglycerol, insulin, leptin and lactate.
source: Furthermore, fasting appreciably lowered concentrations of numerous circulating factors including glucose, triacylglycerol, insulin, leptin and lactate while boosting levels of free fatty acids, corticosterone, beta-hydroxybutyrate and liver triacylglycerol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Fasting boosted levels of free fatty acids, corticosterone, beta-hydroxybutyrate and liver triacylglycerol.
source: Furthermore, fasting appreciably lowered concentrations of numerous circulating factors including glucose, triacylglycerol, insulin, leptin and lactate while boosting levels of free fatty acids, corticosterone, beta-hydroxybutyrate and liver triacylglycerol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: For many of the factors assessed, the degree of modification was exacerbated in the Fasted (48 hr) versus Fasted (18 hr) condition.
source: Importantly, for many of the factors assessed, the degree of modification was exacerbated in the Fasted (48 hr) versus Fasted (18 hr) condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing 18 hr and 48 hr fasting conditions.

claim: ARCAgRP neurons are sensitive to a number of circulating endocrine signals.
source: ARCAgRP neurons are sensitive to a number of circulating endocrine signals (Cowley et al., 2003; Takahashi and Cone, 2005) and display appetite-state and calorie-dependent dynamic activity changes (Betley et al., 2015; Beutler et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Cowley et al., 2003; Takahashi and Cone, 2005).

claim: ARCAgRP neurons display appetite-state and calorie-dependent dynamic activity changes.
source: ARCAgRP neurons are sensitive to a number of circulating endocrine signals (Cowley et al., 2003; Takahashi and Cone, 2005) and display appetite-state and calorie-dependent dynamic activity changes (Betley et al., 2015; Beutler et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Betley et al., 2015; Beutler et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).

claim: Stimulation of ARCAgRP neurons before or during food accessibility drives motivated feeding.
source: Stimulation of these neurons before or during food accessibility drives motivated feeding (Aponte et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2016; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Aponte et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2016; Krashes et al., 2011).

claim: Inhibition of ARCAgRP activity directly attenuates feeding.
source: Conversely, inhibition of ARCAgRP activity directly (Betley et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011; Vardy et al., 2015) or via activation of upstream inhibitory populations (Garfield et al., 2016) attenuates feeding, while postnatal ablation induces starvation (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Betley et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011; Vardy et al., 2015).

claim: Inhibition of ARCAgRP activity via activation of upstream inhibitory populations attenuates feeding.
source: Conversely, inhibition of ARCAgRP activity directly (Betley et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011; Vardy et al., 2015) or via activation of upstream inhibitory populations (Garfield et al., 2016) attenuates feeding, while postnatal ablation induces starvation (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Garfield et al., 2016).

claim: Postnatal ablation of ARCAgRP neurons induces starvation.
source: Conversely, inhibition of ARCAgRP activity directly (Betley et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011; Vardy et al., 2015) or via activation of upstream inhibitory populations (Garfield et al., 2016) attenuates feeding, while postnatal ablation induces starvation (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).

claim: ARCAgRP neurons have the capacity to orchestrate food-seeking to the exclusion of self-preservation and social behaviors.
source: Recent studies demonstrated ARCAgRP neurons have the capacity to orchestrate food-seeking to the exclusion of self-preservation and social behaviors (Burnett et al., 2016; Dietrich et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2016), but deeper behavioral analyses are needed to fully understand this relationship.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Burnett et al., 2016; Dietrich et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2016).

claim: Hunger had a profound effect on a resident male's copulatory advances towards a female conspecific, but only if food was present.
source: First, we found hunger had a profound effect on a resident male's copulatory advances towards a female conspecific, but only if food was present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the resident-female intruder paradigm.

claim: When exposed to a subordinate male intruder, residents displayed less aggression in more intense hunger states, especially when food was present.
source: Similarly, when exposed to a subordinate male intruder, residents displayed less aggression in more intense hunger states; especially when food was present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the resident-male intruder paradigm.

claim: Resident male feeding remained intact in the presence of a male intruder compared to no intrusion.
source: However, in contrast to the reduced food intake of resident males in the presence of a female intruder compared to no intruder, resident male feeding remained intact in the presence of a male intruder compared to no intrusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing feeding behavior in the presence of male versus female intruders.

claim: Resident males showed reduced food intake in the presence of a female intruder compared to no intruder.
source: However, in contrast to the reduced food intake of resident males in the presence of a female intruder compared to no intruder, resident male feeding remained intact in the presence of a male intruder compared to no intrusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the resident-female intruder paradigm.

claim: Sequence analyses of behavioral transitions revealed distinct patterns of behavior in hungry animals in the presence of food, driven primarily by caloric consumption.
source: Sequence analyses of behavioral transitions revealed distinct patterns of behavior in hungry animals in the presence of food, driven primarily by caloric consumption, with the highest degree of behavioral sequence disruption observed during unnatural ARCAgRP stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The highest degree of behavioral sequence disruption was observed during unnatural ARCAgRP stimulation.
source: Sequence analyses of behavioral transitions revealed distinct patterns of behavior in hungry animals in the presence of food, driven primarily by caloric consumption, with the highest degree of behavioral sequence disruption observed during unnatural ARCAgRP stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All states of hunger exhibited comparable patterns of behavior in the absence of food.
source: Remarkably, all states of hunger exhibited comparable patterns of behavior in the absence of food.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intruding receptive females and subordinate males reduced food consumption, independent of appetite state, in an empty or occupied territorialized cage compared to food intake in their homecages.
source: Additionally, we found that intruding receptive females and subordinate males reduced food consumption, independent of appetite state, in an empty or occupied territorialized cage compared to food intake in their homecages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from intruder feeding experiments.

claim: Extreme physiological hunger abrogated female receptivity to male advances.
source: Meanwhile, extreme physiological, but not artificially-induced hunger, abrogated female receptivity to male advances while male intruders' defensive behavior remained analogous across appetite condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from female intruder behavior experiments.

claim: Artificially-induced hunger did not abrogate female receptivity to male advances.
source: Meanwhile, extreme physiological, but not artificially-induced hunger, abrogated female receptivity to male advances while male intruders' defensive behavior remained analogous across appetite condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from female intruder behavior experiments.

claim: Male intruders' defensive behavior remained analogous across appetite condition.
source: Meanwhile, extreme physiological, but not artificially-induced hunger, abrogated female receptivity to male advances while male intruders' defensive behavior remained analogous across appetite condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from male intruder behavior experiments.

claim: In the absence of a female intruder, resident mice demonstrated need-based escalation of food consumption during the Trial Phase.
source: In the absence of a female intruder, resident mice demonstrated need-based escalation of food consumption during the Trial Phase (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Subjects' latency to consume 0.1 grams or five pellets showed similar timescales across all hunger states in the absence of a female intruder.
source: Accordingly, subjects' latency to consume 0.1 grams or five pellets, a metric used to determine homeostatic feeding (see Materials and methods), showed similar timescales across all hunger states (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When a female intruder was present, residents displayed similar grades of food consumption dependent on satiety state.
source: When a female intruder was present, residents displayed similar grades of food consumption dependent on satiety state (Figure 2B): hunger provoked residents to consume more food at a faster rate than the same mice in the Fed state (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Hunger provoked residents to consume more food at a faster rate than the same mice in the Fed state.
source: When a female intruder was present, residents displayed similar grades of food consumption dependent on satiety state (Figure 2B): hunger provoked residents to consume more food at a faster rate than the same mice in the Fed state (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Food intake was significantly attenuated in the presence, compared to the absence, of a female intruder, regardless of appetite condition.
source: However, food intake was significantly attenuated in the presence, compared to the absence, of a female intruder, regardless of appetite condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–F.

claim: Presence of a female intruder was sufficient to right-shift cumulative feeding curves in all conditions tested.
source: Moreover, presence of a female intruder was sufficient to right-shift cumulative feeding curves in all conditions tested (Figure 2C–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 G-K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 G-K.

claim: In both physiological and non-physiologically-induced hunger states, access to a receptive female readjusts goal-seeking and blunts food intake.
source: Therefore, in both physiological and non-physiologically-induced hunger states, access to a receptive female readjusts goal-seeking and blunts food intake.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced food intake in the presence of a female intruder across all hunger states.

claim: Resident food intake was significantly enhanced during the Post-Phase after the intruder female was removed compared to the same mice during this period without prior exposure to the female intruder.
source: We found that resident food intake was significantly enhanced during the Post-Phase after the intruder female was removed compared to the same mice during this period without prior exposure to the female intruder (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F), indicating the delay in the replenishment of caloric balance in the presence of a female intruder is rescued after removal of the female.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F.

claim: The delay in the replenishment of caloric balance in the presence of a female intruder is rescued after removal of the female.
source: We found that resident food intake was significantly enhanced during the Post-Phase after the intruder female was removed compared to the same mice during this period without prior exposure to the female intruder (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F), indicating the delay in the replenishment of caloric balance in the presence of a female intruder is rescued after removal of the female.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased food intake after female removal.

claim: The total duration of mating behaviors, including pursuit, attempted mounting, mounting and intromission decreased with natural hunger intensity in the presence of food.
source: We observed that the total duration of mating behaviors, including pursuit, attempted mounting, mounting and intromission decreased with natural hunger intensity in the presence of food (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cumulative curves to initial mounting attempt depicted higher latencies and a lower number of total animals reaching threshold in the Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions.
source: Cumulative curves to initial mounting attempt also depicted higher latencies and a lower number of total animals reaching threshold in the Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The time spent engaging in mating behavior was lowest in the FedAgRP CS state.
source: Notably, the time spent engaging in mating behavior was lowest in the FedAgRP CS state, an unnatural condition as ARCAgRP neurons should be silent in the presence of food.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mating behavior experiments.

claim: ARCAgRP neurons should be silent in the presence of food.
source: Notably, the time spent engaging in mating behavior was lowest in the FedAgRP CS state, an unnatural condition as ARCAgRP neurons should be silent in the presence of food.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ARCAgRP neuron activity.

claim: Duration of mating behavior was significantly, negatively correlated with the amount of food consumed during the 20 min Trial-Phase across grouped animals.
source: Indeed, duration of mating behavior was significantly, negatively correlated with the amount of food consumed during the 20 min Trial-Phase across grouped animals (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Grooming was positively correlated with mating across grouped animals.
source: Grooming often follows mating behavior, particularly after ejaculation, and we observed a positive correlation between mating and grooming across grouped animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Water intake was strongly correlated with food consumption across grouped animals.
source: Consumption of dry chow drives thirst, thus water intake was strongly correlated with food consumption across grouped animals (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When food was absent, residents showed comparable levels of time spent participating in mating behaviors, regardless of caloric need state tested.
source: However, when we conducted intruder trials where food was absent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E middle panel, bottom), we found that residents showed comparable levels of time spent participating in mating behaviors, regardless of caloric need state tested (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When food was absent, the latency to initially mount the female intruder was reduced and the number of animals engaging in mating behaviors increased in each condition.
source: Additionally, the latency to initially mount the female intruder was reduced and the number of animals engaging in mating behaviors increased in each condition (Figure 2I–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2Q-U).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2Q-U.

claim: Mice in the Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions displayed significantly more time engaging in mating behaviors when food was unavailable compared to when food was available.
source: More specifically, mice that curbed mating behavior when food was available, namely the Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions, displayed significantly more time engaging in mating behaviors when food was unavailable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2L–P.

claim: Preventing animals from sating caloric hunger tipped behavioral choice in favor of sating reproductive drive, the only other satiable motivation at the time.
source: Thus, preventing animals from sating caloric hunger tipped behavioral choice in favor of sating reproductive drive, the only other satiable motivation at the time.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased mating behavior when food was unavailable.

claim: Certain sequences of behavior occurred with high contingency in the Fed state, including the transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission, nose-to-nose chemoinvestigation into ano-genital chemoinvestigation, and mounting/intromission into grooming.
source: Using the Fed group as a baseline, we found that certain sequences of behavior occurred with high contingency in the Fed state, including the transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission, nose-to-nose chemoinvestigation into ano-genital chemoinvestigation, and mounting/intromission into grooming, while others occurred infrequently (Figure 3A, far left).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability to transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission decreased in all hungry animals irrespective of how hunger was elicited.
source: For example, we discovered the probability to transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission or from mounting/intromission into grooming decreased while the probability from eating to eating or drinking to drinking increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how it was elicited (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability to transition from mounting/intromission into grooming decreased in all hungry animals irrespective of how hunger was elicited.
source: For example, we discovered the probability to transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission or from mounting/intromission into grooming decreased while the probability from eating to eating or drinking to drinking increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how it was elicited (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability to transition from eating to eating increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how hunger was elicited.
source: For example, we discovered the probability to transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission or from mounting/intromission into grooming decreased while the probability from eating to eating or drinking to drinking increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how it was elicited (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability to transition from drinking to drinking increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how hunger was elicited.
source: For example, we discovered the probability to transition from pursuit/attempted mounting into mounting/intromission or from mounting/intromission into grooming decreased while the probability from eating to eating or drinking to drinking increased in all hungry animals irrespective of how it was elicited (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The cosine distance between transition frequencies in the Fed state displayed significant differences to all conditions of hunger, with the largest discrepancy seen in the FedAgRP CS condition.
source: During the resident-female intruder paradigm, we found that the cosine distance between transition frequencies in the Fed state displayed significant differences to all conditions of hunger, with the largest discrepancy seen in the FedAgRP CS condition (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cosine distance analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When food was absent, transitions between behaviors across all five conditions remained fairly similar.
source: We also analyzed these sequences in conditions when food was absent. To this end, we calculated average transition frequencies between the remaining six behaviors and found that transitions between behaviors across all five conditions remained fairly similar (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cosine distances from the Fed state were comparable across all natural and artificial hunger states when food was absent.
source: In agreement with this, the cosine distances from the Fed state were comparable across all natural and artificial hunger states (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cosine distance analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All differences from the Fed state were significantly lower when food was absent compared to trials where food was present.
source: Of note, all differences from the Fed state were significantly lower when food was absent compared to trials where food was present (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cosine distance analysis shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: All hunger conditions displayed significantly elevated food consumption compared to the Fed group in the intruder's home cage.
source: As predicted, we observed appetite state-dependent home cage food intake, as all hunger conditions displayed significantly elevated food consumption compared to the Fed group with rapid onset (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: State-dependent stratification of food intake remained in the territorialized, empty male resident cage, but the total amount of food consumed was attenuated.
source: Remarkably, we found that while this state-dependent stratification of food intake remained, the total amount of food consumed was attenuated in the territorialized, empty male resident cage (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,C,E,G,I), accompanied by increased latency to consume 0.1 grams of food and reduced number of animals meeting this threshold (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,D,F,H,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Food intake and rate of consumption were further mitigated in the territorialized, occupied male resident cage.
source: Moreover, food intake and rate of consumption were further mitigated in the territorialized, occupied male resident cage (Figure 4B,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–J.

claim: A familiar pattern of feeding behavior emerged depending on the intensity of deprivation during the Post-Phase after the male resident had been removed from the cage.
source: Finally, when assessing food intake in the Post-Phase after the male resident had been removed from the cage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, right panel), we found a familiar pattern of feeding behavior emerge depending on the intensity of deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Severe food deprivation is known to disrupt ovulation rate, cyclic behavior, and reproductive receptivity.
source: Although severe food deprivation is known to disrupt ovulation rate, cyclic behavior, and reproductive receptivity (Cooper et al., 1970; Howland, 1971), we still confirmed all female intruders were in estrus before the resident female-intruder assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Cooper et al., 1970; Howland, 1971).

claim: A clear reduction in the duration of receptivity behavior and total number of subjects engaging in receptive behaviors was observed in Fasted (48 hr) mice that differed from all other groups tested.
source: We observed a clear reduction in the duration of receptivity behavior and total number of subjects engaging in receptive behaviors in Fasted (48 hr) mice that differed from all other groups tested (Figure 4F–G), while the duration of time spent engaging in non-receptive (escape/attempted escape) behaviors was comparable across conditions (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F–G.

claim: The duration of time spent engaging in non-receptive (escape/attempted escape) behaviors was comparable across conditions.
source: We observed a clear reduction in the duration of receptivity behavior and total number of subjects engaging in receptive behaviors in Fasted (48 hr) mice that differed from all other groups tested (Figure 4F–G), while the duration of time spent engaging in non-receptive (escape/attempted escape) behaviors was comparable across conditions (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Food intake measurements in the male residents in the absence of a male intruder affirmed both physiological and artificially-induced hunger stimulate feeding coincident on need.
source: Food intake measurements in the male residents in the absence of a male intruder affirmed both physiological and artificially-induced hunger stimulate feeding coincident on need (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The latency to eat 0.1 grams (five pellets) of chow was comparable across the natural and artificial hunger states with each mouse meeting this threshold.
source: Reflective of this consummatory behavior, the latency to eat 0.1 grams (five pellets) of chow was comparable across the natural and artificial hunger states with each mouse meeting this threshold (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A similar pattern of food intake was present contingent on caloric need state in the presence of a male intruder.
source: As in the resident-female intruder paradigm above, a similar pattern of food intake was present contingent on caloric need state in the presence of a male intruder (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When a male intruder was introduced into the resident's cage, the total amount of food consumed by the resident mice did not vary much from the no intruder condition.
source: However, unlike our findings in the resident-female intruder paradigm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–F), when a male intruder was introduced into the resident's cage, the total amount of food consumed by the resident mice did not vary much from the no intruder condition (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Latency curves remained comparable in the presence or absence of a male intruder.
source: These results were echoed by the cumulative latency to consume 0.1 grams of food, as latency curves remained comparable in the presence or absence of a male intruder (Figure 5C–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–K.

claim: A subordinate male stimulus was insufficient to curtail total food consumption across appetite states.
source: Therefore, unlike a female intruder, a subordinate male stimulus was insufficient to curtail total food consumption across appetite states.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no significant difference in food intake with or without a male intruder.

claim: All groups of resident animals, regardless of hunger state, consumed more food during the Post-Phase after the intruder male was removed compared to the same period following a Trial Phase in the absence of a male intruder.
source: In the Post-Phase after the intruder male was removed from the cage, all groups of resident animals, regardless of hunger state, consumed more food compared to the same period following a Trial Phase in the absence of a male intruder (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions displayed the lowest level of territorial aggression.
source: Of all the conditions tested, Fasted (48 hr) and FedAgRP CS conditions displayed the lowest level of territorial aggression, reflected by the total duration of time (Figure 5H), bout number (data not shown) and total number of residents aggressing intruder mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and 5I.

claim: The speed at which the residents aggress the intruder is slightly longer in conditions of hunger.
source: Although the latency to attack is quick, the speed at which the residents aggress the intruder is slightly longer in conditions of hunger (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The residents in the male intruder assay demonstrated a positive correlation between drinking duration and food consumed.
source: However, the residents in the male intruder assay demonstrated a positive correlation between drinking duration and food consumed (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Aggression behavioral architecture was more similar across appetite states in the absence of food where animals exhibited comparable amounts of aggressive behaviors toward a male intruder.
source: Aggression behavioral architecture was more similar across appetite states in the absence of food where animals exhibited comparable amounts of aggressive behaviors toward a male intruder (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: When feeding was unattainable, latency to aggress male intruders occurred faster and every subject tested demonstrated aggressive behaviors toward male intruders when compared to the same residents in the presence of food.
source: When feeding was unattainable, latency to aggress male intruders occurred faster and every subject tested demonstrated aggressive behaviors toward male intruders when compared to the same residents in the presence of food (Figure 5I–J; Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q–U).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q–U.

claim: Fasted (48 hr) animals significantly escalated the duration spent aggressing a male intruder in the absence versus presence of food.
source: Fasted (48 hr) animals significantly escalated the duration spent aggressing a male intruder in the absence versus presence of food, while the degrees of aggression expressed in all other groups were comparable independent of food accessibility (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1L–P.

claim: The degrees of aggression expressed in all other groups were comparable independent of food accessibility.
source: Fasted (48 hr) animals significantly escalated the duration spent aggressing a male intruder in the absence versus presence of food, while the degrees of aggression expressed in all other groups were comparable independent of food accessibility (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1L–P.

claim: The probability to transition from chasing into aggression decreased in escalating conditions of hunger.

claim: In rodents, the context of a social interaction, including territorial ownership and hunger state, can prominently guide how behavioral encounters will unfold.
source: Overall, we have demonstrated more dynamic interaction between two mutually exclusive motivations – hunger and social interaction – than has previously been appreciated in recent neuroscience research. We have shown that in rodents, the context of a social interaction, including territorial ownership and hunger state, can prominently guide how behavioral encounters will unfold.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A history of winning previous territorial encounters increases the probability of aggressive behaviors.
source: A separate cohort of male residents was prepared as described above (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), and these sexually-experienced animals were provided with subordinate mice to aggress before trials were conducted to gain fighting experience and establish dominance in their home cage, as a history of winning previous territorial encounters increases the probability of aggressive behaviors (Barnett and Spencer, 1951; Calhoun, 1963; Crowcroft, 1955; Crowcroft, 1966; Crowcroft and Rowe, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Barnett and Spencer, 1951; Calhoun, 1963; Crowcroft, 1955; Crowcroft, 1966; Crowcroft and Rowe, 1963).

claim: Subordination is highly dependent on housing status, age, size and fighting experience.
source: Ad libitum fed, group-housed males ranging from 5 to 8 weeks old and 15–22 grams without fighting experience were selected to serve as intruders (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) as subordination is highly dependent on housing status, age, size and fighting experience (Crowcroft, 1955; Crowcroft, 1966; Crowcroft and Rowe, 1963; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Crowcroft, 1955; Crowcroft, 1966; Crowcroft and Rowe, 1963; Yang et al., 2017).

claim: Male mice often engage in post-coital grooming behavior following an encounter with a receptive female.
source: While male mice often engage in post-coital grooming behavior following an encounter with a receptive female, they fail to show post-fight grooming after engagement with an intruding male as the dominant animal is often uninjured during the confrontation (Barnett and Spencer, 1951; Crowcroft, 1955; Crowcroft and Rowe, 1963).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse behavior.
